source: OECD (2025), Health at a Glance 2025: OECD Indicators, OECD Publishing, Paris
framing: Gap framing: every figure is what is NOT covered, NOT satisfied or unmet. Gap figures are 100 minus the published figure.
rule: HAL may phrase these facts freely but must not state any figure, ranking or claim that is not in this list. Verbatim report sentences may name other countries; only what they say about this country may be used.

facts.text: 47% of people in Lithuania were NOT satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare where they live in 2024, versus an OECD average of 36%.
32.7% of health spending in Lithuania was NOT covered by government or compulsory insurance schemes in 2023, versus an OECD average of 24.9%.
4.3% of people in Lithuania reported unmet medical care needs due to cost, distance or waiting times in 2024 (average of 28 OECD countries: 3.4%).
7% of hospital care costs in Lithuania were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 11% on average in the OECD.
28% of outpatient medical care costs in Lithuania were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 22% on average in the OECD.
88% of dental care costs in Lithuania were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 68% on average in the OECD.
49% of pharmaceutical costs in Lithuania were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 42% on average in the OECD.
This is especially notable in Finland, Lithuania, Ireland, Greece, Spain and France, where unmet medical care needs due to waiting times increased by 1.4 percentage points or more since 2019.

This varies considerably across OECD countries, from fewer than 2% of households experiencing catastrophic health spending in Sweden, Slovenia, the United Kingdom, Ireland and the Netherlands, to over 10% of households in Lithuania, Latvia and Hungary (Figure 5.10).
In Lithuania, while there were 6.6 doctors per 1 000 population in metropolitan areas, there were only two doctors per 1 000 in remote areas.

In 2023, PHC represented 14% of all health spending on average across OECD countries, ranging from 10% or less in Switzerland, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and the Slovak Republic to around 20% in Lithuania, Estonia and Finland (Figure 7.16).
In Lithuania and Estonia, the large share of PHC in overall health spending can be explained by spending on dental care.
